# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Obstetric emergencies, injuries, strokes and myocardial infarctions share a
geographical condition: the patient has to reach a hospital able to treat them
in time. The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery measured timely access as the
share of the population that can reach, within two hours, a facility able to
perform caesarean delivery, laparotomy and treatment of open fractures
[@meara2015], and the Lancet Global Health Commission on high-quality health
systems counted timely action among the components of competent care, with
access as a prerequisite for benefiting from it [@kruk2018]. Global friction surfaces have made it
possible to map travel time everywhere: about 8.9 % of the world population
cannot reach a health facility within one hour by motorized transport, and
43.3 % cannot on foot [@weiss2020]. National studies built on similar models
report, for instance, that 29.0 % of people in sub-Saharan Africa live more than
two hours from a public hospital [@ouma2018] and that access falls steeply from
cities to villages and dispersed rural areas [@florio2023]; others combine travel
time with the burden of surgical disease [@juran2018].

These figures depend on how access is measured. Access is a multidimensional
concept [@penchansky1981], and its spatial component alone requires a chain of
decisions: a metric (straight-line distance, network distance or travel time),
an access model (the nearest facility or a floating catchment that weighs supply
against demand), a set of destinations, and a population unit with its
weighting [@guagliardo2004; @wang2012; @neutens2015]. Each link can change the
result. Accessibility computed from areal centroids carries aggregation error
[@hewko2002; @apparicio2008; @apparicio2017], raster and network models
identify the same underserved areas but count different numbers of people in
them [@delamater2012], and aggregate statistics shift with the areal units used
[@openshaw1984; @fotheringham1991]. In rural Haiti five measures of access to
public hospitals correlated at 0.78 to 0.99, yet straight-line distance
overstated the population covered within a given threshold [@bhangdia2022].

Two gaps follow for national planning in low- and middle-income countries.
First, measures are usually compared through correlations, whereas the planning
output is a list: the districts classified as underserved. Two measures can rank
districts almost identically and still disagree on which ones cross a threshold.
Second, modeled travel time is rarely tested against an outcome it should
explain. Validation is typically internal, or against routing services that
share the same road data [@nelson2019]. In Spain, longer car travel time to
hospitals was associated with higher mortality, most clearly among older adults
and for time-sensitive causes [@perez2026]. Comparable tests in settings with
fragmented health systems and long travel times are scarce.

Peru is such a setting. Its territory spans a coastal desert, the Andes above
3,500 m and the lowland Amazon. Its health system runs separate networks for
the Ministry of Health and regional governments, the social-security insurer,
the armed forces and police, and private providers, and the extension of
coverage has long been its main challenge [@alcalde2011]. Two national
studies have modeled travel time to care. Carrasco-Escobar et al. [-@carrasco2020]
estimated village-level times to public facilities of three levels of care, but
did not weight by population or compare their estimates with other measures or
with observed journeys. Bocanegra-Becerra [-@bocanegra2025] estimated that
42.4 % of the population could not reach public neurosurgical care within four
hours. The 2025 census now provides population counts for every district.

This study addresses three questions. RQ1: how far, in person-weighted travel
time, do Peruvians live from the nearest public complex hospital, and where are
those beyond 60 and 120 minutes? RQ2: how much does the identification of
districts with deficient access depend on the metric, the population
aggregation, the access model and the destination set? RQ3: is the measure
associated with an independent outcome, death outside a health facility,
particularly for causes amenable to hospital care? The study contributes, first,
a reproducible district measure weighted by the 2025 census and checked against
an alternative routing engine; second, evidence that aggregation and the access
model, rather than the choice of destinations, change which districts are
flagged; and third, a pre-specified negative test that shows the limits of place
of death as a criterion for validating access measures. The analysis plan was
version-controlled before the data were analyzed, and every deviation from it is
reported with its timing (Appendix A).

# Background {#sec-background}

## Why measures of access disagree

Distance-based measures summarize the impedance between a population and its
nearest facility; gravity and floating catchment measures add supply and
competing demand. The two-step floating catchment area method (2SFCA) computes,
for each facility, a supply-to-demand ratio within a travel-time catchment and
then sums the ratios reachable from each population location [@luo2003];
enhanced versions weight both steps by distance decay [@luo2009]. Because
nearest-facility and catchment measures answer different questions, proximity
versus availability, they need not agree. Reviews have repeatedly asked that
the choice be justified rather than assumed [@wang2012; @neutens2015].

The population unit adds a second layer of variation. Accessibility computed at
the centroid of an areal unit stands in for every resident of that unit. In
Montreal, centroid-based measures were accurate for most census tracts but
produced important errors for 5–10 % of them, mostly in the suburbs, where
residents are spread unevenly [@apparicio2008], and a later comparison found
errors of the same order [@apparicio2017]. Aggregation error arises whenever a
single point stands for a population spread across an area, and finer data on
where people live within each unit reduce it [@hewko2002]; it is the local form
of the modifiable areal unit problem [@openshaw1984]. Peru's
districts range from city blocks to Amazonian territories of thousands of square
kilometers, so this problem cannot be assumed away.

## Validating national travel-time maps

Friction surfaces convert land cover, roads, slope and water into the time
needed to cross each cell, and accumulate cost from the destinations
[@weiss2018; @weiss2020]. Several studies have set their estimates against
routing services and reported journeys. Against Google driving directions, the
global accessibility indicators were shorter in most journeys, with a median
difference of $-16.9$ % [@nelson2019]. Women in rural Rwanda reported journeys to
a district hospital 1.49 times longer than modeled [@rudolfson2020], and in
Lagos replicated drives to emergency obstetric care took a median of 50 minutes,
against 5 minutes from a friction surface and 11 minutes from OpenStreetMap
routing [@bankethomas2021]. Agreement in ranking does not, therefore, imply
agreement in minutes, and the error is largest in congested cities and where
transport is not motorized.

## Access and where people die

Most death registration systems record the place of death, and studies of
end-of-life care use it as an indicator. Its determinants extend well beyond
distance: among people with cancer, home death is associated with low functional
status, patient preference, home care and family support [@gomes2006], and in Latin
America with older age, lower education and, in some countries, rural residence
[@cordoba2026]. In Peru, 41.3 % of deaths registered between 2017 and 2024
occurred at home, with marked differences by insurance, education, ethnicity and
department [@mirandachavez2026]. Whether modeled travel time adds to these
determinants has not been tested in Peru. If it does, place of death could serve
as an external check on access measures, which is the test RQ3 sets out.

# Study area and data {#sec-data}

Peru had 32,706,028 counted residents in 1,893 districts in the 2025 census
[@inei2026]. <!-- claim-16 --> Districts are the smallest political-administrative
unit, and they are highly unequal in size and population. The
analysis combines eight data sources (Table @tbl-data). Destinations are public
complex hospitals, defined as Ministry of Health and regional-government
facilities of category II-1 or above in the national registry of health
establishments [@renipress2026]; the registry lists their institution, category
and coordinates. Population counts come from the census and are distributed
within districts with the 2025 WorldPop constrained grid [@bondarenko2025;
@tatem2017]. Travel time uses the 2020 motorized and walking-only friction
surfaces of the Malaria Atlas Project [@weiss2020]. District polygons come from
the Common Operational Dataset of administrative boundaries [@ocha2025]: of the
1,893 census districts, 21 have no polygon (294,298 residents, mostly districts
created after 2017) and one polygon, a boundary area between Mazamari and
Pangoa, has no census row. District mean altitude comes from the Copernicus
DEM [@esa2022]. The analysis therefore covers 1,872 districts and
32,411,730 people, 99.1 % of the counted population. <!-- claim-16 --> Deaths
come from the national online death certificate system [@sinadef2026], whose
national roll-out is described by Vargas-Herrera et al. [-@vargas2018].

# Methods {#sec-methods}

Fig. @fig-workflow summarizes the workflow. Every number reported below is
produced by a version-controlled pipeline run on Colab, and every figure and
table is generated from its outputs.

![Data sources, measurement, checks and the three research questions.](media/Fig1_workflow.pdf){#fig-workflow width=1}

## Destinations and population

We restricted destinations to the public network of the Ministry of Health
and regional governments, open to the general population; social-security,
armed-forces and police hospitals serve their affiliates and private hospitals
charge fees. Alternative destination sets enter the sensitivity analysis. Of the 182 geolocated public complex hospitals, 172 lay inside their
own district polygon and 7 within 20 km of its boundary. Two lay more than
200 km away, an error in their coordinates, and were excluded from the main set;
re-placing them at their district centroid changed the 60-minute class of
1.12 % of districts (pre-specified limit 5 %). One hospital belonged to a
district without a polygon. <!-- claim-17, claim-3 --> The 180 hospitals in the
main set occupy 174 grid cells. <!-- claim-17 -->

We allocated census counts to the cells of a 30 arc-second grid (about 927 m)
in proportion to the WorldPop estimates, so that each district keeps its census
total exactly; this dasymetric step follows the logic of the WorldPop models
themselves [@stevens2015] while anchoring the totals to the census.

## Travel time and district summaries

We computed travel time from every cell to the nearest hospital as a
multi-source accumulated cost over the motorized friction surface with
Dijkstra's algorithm [@dijkstra1959; @virtanen2020], with cell widths corrected
for latitude and the friction resampled to the grid by nearest neighbor. For
each district we report the person-weighted mean travel time and the share of
residents whose cells lie beyond 60 and 120 minutes. The 60-minute threshold is
the main one, as in global reporting [@weiss2020]; 120 minutes, the surgical
access benchmark [@meara2015], is secondary because the convergent check showed
weak agreement on that class (Section @sec-res-osrm). We also report the
district-weighted mean, to show how much the headline changes when every
district counts equally, and the share of people living in districts whose
person-weighted mean exceeds each threshold, the unit at which planning lists
are usually drawn. We group districts by the Amazon basin, from HydroBASINS
level 4 [@lehner2013], and by mean altitude: below 500 m, 500–2,500 m, and the
high (2,500–3,500 m) and very high ($\geq$ 3,500 m) altitude classes of Barry and
Pollard [-@barry2003].

## Convergent check against routing

We routed a pre-specified sample of 200 district centroids, stratified by
quintile of travel time, by car to their three nearest hospitals with OSRM
[@luxen2011] and kept the shortest time; a second, enriched sample of 150
districts with mean travel time above 45 minutes probes the remote tail. Both
engines rest on OpenStreetMap roads, so this is a check of convergent, not
independent, validity [@osm2026]. The pre-specified rule required a Spearman correlation
of at least 0.80 outside the Amazon; at the time, the Amazon was proxied by five
departments, and we report the basin split as a post hoc refinement. Six
pairs of departmental capitals were compared in the same way.

## Sensitivity to the measure (RQ2)

Against the main measure we compared ten variants. Two use straight-line
distance, from the district centroid and population-weighted. One reads the
travel time at the district's center cell, without population weighting, to
isolate aggregation (the pre-specified check of whether weighting matters,
refuted if Spearman $\geq$ 0.95). One multiplies travel time by the OSRM-to-friction
ratio of its trip-length band. Three widen the destination set (adding
social-security hospitals, all complex hospitals, and uncategorised
hospital-like facilities). One uses the walking-only surface. Two compute a
2SFCA score [@luo2003] with 60- and 120-minute catchments, with supply equal to
the number of hospitals in each cell of a grid four times coarser than the main
one, read as a person-weighted district mean.

For each variant we report Spearman's correlation with a bootstrap 95 % CI over
districts, Kendall's tau, the Jaccard overlap of the 100 worst-access districts,
and Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960] for the deficient-access class at 60 and
120 minutes. Variants in minutes use the same thresholds; variants in other
units flag the same number of districts as the main measure, so that kappa
compares classifications rather than units. Under the pre-specified
criterion, Spearman $\geq$ 0.95 together with kappa $\geq$ 0.90 for straight-line distance
would have shown that travel time adds nothing to it.

## Need and spatial structure

We summarized need as the sum of the z-scores of the census share of residents
aged 60 or over and the share aged 5 or over with a disability, with equal
weights. A district is high-need if the sum is positive and has deficient access
if its person-weighted mean exceeds 60 minutes. We assessed stability across
five weighting schemes; a composite ranking was to be reported only if Kendall's
tau between schemes reached 0.80. Spatial clustering of person-weighted travel
time was tested with global Moran's I and local indicators of spatial
association [@anselin1995] under queen contiguity and four and eight nearest
neighbors, with 9,999 permutations and false-discovery-rate control
[@benjamini1995], using PySAL [@rey2022].

## External outcome test (RQ3)

The outcome is death outside a health facility (at home, on a public road or in
another non-facility place) among deaths registered in 2022–2025, assigned to
the district of residence. The main population, fixed before the death records
were read, is deaths from causes amenable to timely hospital care, adapted from
the concept of amenable mortality [@nolte2003]: acute conditions (myocardial
infarction, stroke and obstetric causes) and chronic conditions (diabetes,
hypertensive disease, chronic lower respiratory disease and chronic kidney
disease). H3a states that longer travel time increases the odds of dying outside
a facility; H3b, that the gradient is steeper for acute than for chronic causes.

We fitted a logistic regression with department fixed effects and
district-clustered standard errors, giving a population-averaged odds ratio per
60 minutes, adjusted for age group, sex, cause group and district mean altitude
[@cameron2015; @mundlak1978]. Sensitivity analyses comprise a generalized
estimating equation with exchangeable correlation [@liang1986], the exclusion of
districts with low registration completeness, the exclusion of the unclassified
"other place" category, the period 2020–2021, a within-department permutation
placebo (200 permutations), and cancer deaths as a negative control. A
simulation with known truth, with district random intercepts and the observed
baseline odds, estimated the false-positive rate, bias and coverage of the
estimator, following Morris et al. [-@morris2019]; the plan required a
false-positive rate of at most 7 % for confirmatory use.

## Analysis plan, deviations and software

The plan was frozen in a version-controlled file before any access result was
computed and amended in dated versions; it was not deposited in a public
registry, so we describe it as pre-specified rather than pre-registered.
Appendix A lists each deviation, when it was declared, and why. Two
machine-learning checks were subordinate to the main analysis: a ridge
calibration of the OSRM-to-friction ratio, used only as a sensitivity variant,
and a gradient-boosting test of whether travel time improves the prediction of
place of death; both were validated by leaving one department out
[@roberts2017; @ploton2020]. Models used statsmodels [@seabold2010] and
scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011]. Code, the cached routing responses and the
notebook that reproduces every output are archived in a public repository
(reference withheld for anonymized review).

# Results {#sec-results}

## How far people live from a public complex hospital {#sec-res-rq1}

The person-weighted mean travel time to the nearest public complex hospital was
37.8 minutes; 10.9 % of residents lived in cells more than 60 minutes away and
4.6 % more than 120 minutes away. Weighting every district equally raised the
mean to 91.6 minutes, because the most remote districts are small. The share
also depends on the unit that is classified: 12.5 % of people lived in districts
whose person-weighted mean exceeded 60 minutes, and 5.5 % in districts above
120 minutes. <!-- claim-1, claim-3 --> On foot, 46.5 % of residents lived more
than 60 minutes from such a hospital, and the person-weighted mean was
226.8 minutes. <!-- claim-14 -->

Long travel times concentrate where few people live (Fig. @fig-access a). Within
60 minutes, coverage was 93.1 % below 500 m, 88.2 % at 2,500–3,500 m, 85.6 % at
3,500 m or more and 83.8 % at 500–2,500 m; the last band, which spans inter-Andean
valleys and the forested slopes towards the Amazon, also had the lowest
coverage within 120 minutes (91.9 %, Fig. @fig-access b). <!-- claim-22 --> The
very high Andes differ in a subtler way: only 66.0 % of their residents were
within 30 minutes, the lowest of any band, but 97.4 % were within two hours.
<!-- claim-22 --> Inside the Amazon basin, 22.8 % of residents lived more than
60 minutes away, against 5.6 % outside it, and in the lowland basin below 500 m
the person-weighted mean reached 274.2 minutes (Table @tbl-equity).
<!-- claim-23 -->

## Agreement with routing {#sec-res-osrm}

Of the 200 pre-specified centroids, 199 were routed. Overall, friction and OSRM
times correlated at Spearman 0.738. Outside the five Amazon departments, the
stratum to which the pre-specified rule applied, the correlation was 0.801
(95 % CI 0.733–0.854, n = 174): the point estimate met the 0.80 threshold, but
the interval crosses it. With the HydroBASINS basin, agreement was 0.850
outside the basin (n = 86) and 0.653 inside it (n = 113); within the basin it
was 0.705 above 500 m (n = 96) and 0.513 in the lowland (n = 17, 95 % CI $-0.057$
to 0.919). In the enriched remote sample it fell to 0.400 (n = 149).
<!-- claim-2 --> OSRM times were longer than friction times in the
pre-specified sample (median ratio 1.17) and shorter in the lowland basin
(0.82), where the friction surface has no river transport and OSRM snaps
centroids to the nearest road. <!-- claim-18 --> The two engines agreed weakly on
the 120-minute class (kappa 0.342 across both samples). <!-- claim-1 --> For six
pairs of departmental capitals the mean absolute difference between engines was
18.0 % (Supplementary Table S1 and Fig. S1). <!-- claim-18 -->

## Which districts each measure flags {#sec-res-rq2}

The destination set barely mattered: adding social-security hospitals, all
complex hospitals or uncategorised hospital-like facilities kept Spearman at
0.991–0.993 and kappa at 60 minutes at 0.978–0.990 (Table @tbl-rq2).
<!-- claim-10 --> The other choices mattered more.

Straight-line distance ranked districts much as travel time did (Spearman 0.902
from the centroid and 0.923 population-weighted) but agreed less on who is
deficient. When each flagged the same 746 districts at 60 minutes, kappa was
0.739 and 0.777, and the top-100 worst-access sets overlapped by only 0.429 and
0.351. <!-- claim-9 --> In the population-weighted comparison, 100 districts were
flagged by travel time alone and another 100 by straight-line distance alone,
the latter cut at the matched distance of 33.1 km (Fig. @fig-methods).
<!-- claim-19 --> The two groups lie in different terrain: 79 of the districts
flagged only by travel time are in the Amazon basin and 52 lie at 500–2,500 m,
whereas 57 of those flagged only by distance lie at 3,500 m or more.
<!-- claim-19 -->

Aggregation changed the count more than the ranking. Travel time read at the
district's center cell correlated with the person-weighted measure at 0.810
(95 % CI 0.788–0.830), below the 0.95 at which the simpler measure would have
sufficed, and it flagged 1,010 districts instead of 746 at 60 minutes, and 537
instead of 235 at 120 minutes. <!-- claim-13 --> Walking time ranked districts
like motorized time (0.958) but, at the same threshold, flagged 1,686 of the
1,872 districts. <!-- claim-14 -->

The catchment model departed furthest. The 2SFCA score correlated with travel
time at 0.524 with a 60-minute catchment and 0.306 with a 120-minute catchment,
and flagging the same number of districts gave kappa of 0.539 and 0.271. With
the 60-minute catchment, 14.9 % of districts, holding 4.2 % of the population,
had no hospital within reach and a score of zero; those districts agreed with
the travel-time class at kappa 0.418. <!-- claim-11 --> Under the pre-specified
criteria, straight-line distance did not reproduce the travel-time
classification (Spearman below 0.95 and kappa below 0.90), and population
weighting was not redundant.

## Need and spatial structure {#sec-res-need}

Combining need with access, 371 districts, home to 739,935 people (2.3 % of the
population), were high-need with deficient access (Fig. @fig-need); 86.3 % of
them lie at 2,500 m or more. <!-- claim-12, claim-21 --> Membership of this group
was stable across the five need-weighting schemes (97.3 %), but the need index
itself was not: the minimum Kendall's tau against the equal-weight ranking was
0.729, below the 0.80 the plan required, so we report membership and no
composite ranking. Travel time was strongly clustered (global Moran's I 0.662
with queen contiguity, 0.656 and 0.547 with four and eight neighbors; p = 0.0001
with 9,999 permutations), but the number of significant local clusters varied
from 235 to 456 districts across neighborhood definitions, so local clusters
are not reported as findings. <!-- claim-12 -->

![Need and access by district. Need: sum of the z-scores of the shares aged 60 or over and with a disability; deficient access: person-weighted mean travel time above 60 min. The key gives the number of districts and the share of the population in each class. The blank polygon (Mazamari–Pangoa) has no census row. Map lines delineate study areas and do not necessarily depict accepted national boundaries.](media/Fig4_need_access.pdf){#fig-need width=0.46}

## Travel time and dying outside a facility {#sec-res-rq3}

Of 601,092 deaths registered in 2022–2025, 593,438 had a usable district of
residence and place of death; 590,654 had the district resolved by name, and
70,496 of these were due to amenable causes. <!-- claim-20 --> Among amenable
deaths, travel time was not associated with dying outside a facility: the odds
ratio per 60 minutes was 1.005 (95 % CI 0.986–1.025, p = 0.607), and the
within-department placebo gave p = 0.61 (Fig. @fig-rq3). <!-- claim-4, claim-20 -->
The estimate stayed near one when low-completeness districts or the "other
place" category were excluded and in 2020–2021. The exchangeable GEE gave 0.992
(0.977–1.009); its sign is opposite to the main estimate, so the pre-specified
"same sign" criterion was not met, although neither estimator detected an
association. <!-- claim-24 --> The acute and chronic gradients did not differ
(odds ratios 1.000 and 1.020; interaction p = 0.251; Supplementary Table S4). <!-- claim-24 -->

![Odds ratios of dying outside a health facility per 60 minutes of travel time, with 95 % CIs. H3a: amenable causes (pre-specified) and its sensitivity analyses; H3b: acute and chronic amenable causes; other cause groups; all causes (exploratory). The dashed line marks the odds ratio planted in the simulation.](media/Fig5_rq3.pdf){#fig-rq3 width=1}

Over all causes the odds ratio was 1.037 (1.023–1.052), but this exploratory
gradient was not specific to access-sensitive causes: it was driven by the
residual "other" group (1.053, 1.034–1.071), and cancer, the negative control,
showed a similar non-significant estimate (1.032, 0.978–1.090). <!-- claim-5 -->
Two diagnostics bound the interpretation. In the known-truth simulation the
estimator had a false-positive rate of 7.6 % (Monte Carlo SE 1.2 %), above the
pre-specified 7 %, and 90.0 % coverage at a planted odds ratio of 1.10, which it
detected with power 0.99 (Supplementary Table S2); by the plan's rule the model
is therefore used descriptively, not for confirmatory inference. <!-- claim-6, claim-24 --> Second,
the cause was unknown more often for deaths outside facilities, most of all near
hospitals (22.5 % against 12.9 % in facilities within 30 minutes; 11.3 % against
9.1 % beyond 120 minutes; Supplementary Table S5). <!-- claim-15 --> If
unknown-cause deaths are amenable in similar proportion across travel times,
excluding them removes more outside deaths near hospitals, which would steepen
rather than flatten the gradient. A gradient-boosting model gained no predictive
value from travel time among amenable deaths (change in Brier score $-0.00292$,
95 % CI $-0.00574$ to $-0.00012$; Supplementary Table S3). <!-- claim-8 -->

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Aggregation and the access model change the list of underserved districts

The headline is robust to the definition of destinations and fragile to the
choices that define the population and the access model. That ordering matches
what Apparicio et al. [-@apparicio2008; -@apparicio2017] found for urban health
services, where straight-line and network distances correlated above 0.90 but the
choice of accessibility measure changed the assessment most, and what Delamater et al.
[-@delamater2012] found in Michigan, where raster and network models placed the
limited-access areas in the same places but counted different numbers of people
in them. Peru magnifies the aggregation component. Centroid-based travel time
erred for 5–10 % of census tracts in Montreal; here, reading time at the
district center instead of weighting by where people live flagged 264 more
districts at 60 minutes, because large Andean and Amazonian districts have their
population concentrated in a valley or along a river while their geometric center
lies in empty terrain. <!-- claim-13 --> Ranking correlations alone would have
hidden this: Bhangdia et al. [-@bhangdia2022] warned that highly correlated
measures can still disagree on coverage, and our straight-line comparison shows
the same pattern at the threshold that planners use. The disagreement is
geographically structured rather than random. Travel time adds districts on the
forested Andean slopes, where distance understates the cost of crossing terrain,
and straight-line distance adds districts on the high plateau, where roads make
travel faster than distance suggests.

The catchment model answers a different question. 2SFCA rewards districts whose
catchment holds several hospitals relative to its population, so a district one
hour from a single hospital that serves a large city can score lower than a
remote district near a small one. Florio et al. [-@florio2023] concluded for
sub-Saharan Africa that geographic access is constrained mainly by travel
impedance rather than by facility density. Our results suggest a corollary for
planning: proximity and availability rank Peruvian districts differently
(Spearman 0.306–0.524), so a priority list should state which of the two it
targets. <!-- claim-11 -->

## What the routing check can and cannot show

The friction surface ranked districts consistently with OSRM outside the Amazon,
at the pre-specified threshold, but the agreement weakened in the remote tail
and in the lowland basin. Two mechanisms are visible in the data. The surface
lacks river transport, which dominates in the lowland Amazon, and OSRM snaps a
centroid to the nearest road and ignores the leg from it, which makes remote
districts look closer. Since both engines rely on OpenStreetMap roads, their
agreement is convergent evidence, not an independent validation. External
studies suggest that both kinds of model underestimate real journeys:
self-reported times were 1.49 times the modeled ones in rural Rwanda
[@rudolfson2020], and modeled times in Lagos fell far short of replicated
drives [@bankethomas2021]. Our absolute minutes should therefore be read as
optimistic for people without a vehicle and for river-dependent districts, and
the 120-minute class, on which the engines agreed weakly, as indicative only.
<!-- claim-1 --> The walking estimate gives the other bound: for residents who
must walk, 46.5 % of the population lives more than an hour from a public complex
hospital. <!-- claim-14 -->

## Why place of death did not validate access

The external test did not find what a valid access measure should produce, a
gradient specific to causes amenable to hospital care. Three explanations are
compatible with the data, and the study cannot separate them. First, place of
death is a poor marker of geographic access in Peru. Its national pattern is
shaped by insurance, education, ethnicity, preference and palliative-care needs
[@mirandachavez2026; @gomes2006], and the Latin American evidence links home
death more consistently to age and education than to rurality [@cordoba2026].
Second, exposure is measured at the district of residence, not on the journey of
each patient. This ecological assignment is subject to the uncertain geographic
context problem [@kwan2012] and dilutes any individual-level association, and
the simulation did not model that dilution. Third, the measure itself may err
most where an association would be strongest, in the remote tail. In contrast,
Pérez et al. [-@perez2026] found that hospital travel time was associated with
mortality in Spain, a high-income country with universal coverage, using
mortality rather than the place of death of those who died. The two
results are not contradictory, but together they suggest that place of death is
a weak criterion for validating access measures. The null result here is
informative within its precision. The interval excludes an odds ratio of 1.10
per hour, an effect the simulation detected with power 0.99, but it does not
rule out smaller associations, and the estimator's false-positive rate exceeded
the pre-specified limit. <!-- claim-4, claim-6 -->

## Implications for planning

The results support three practical rules for the agencies that rank districts
for hospital investment. Population-weighted travel time should replace both
straight-line distance and centroid-based measures when lists are drawn, because
those two produce different lists, not just a slightly different ranking.
Priority lists should be presented with the access model they assume, since
proximity and availability point to different districts. And the 371 high-need
districts with deficient access, mostly above 2,500 m, are a defensible starting
set because their membership was stable across need weightings; no single
composite ranking within that set is warranted. <!-- claim-12, claim-21 -->
These rules rest on RQ1 and RQ2 only; RQ3 provides no basis for prioritizing
districts by place of death.

## Limitations

The friction surface dates from 2020, whereas hospitals are listed as of 2026
and deaths span 2022–2025; facilities opened or closed in between are not
represented in the exposure. Hospitals without coordinates in the registry could
not be placed. The 21 census districts without a polygon (294,298 residents) are
excluded; dropping the 12 provinces that contain them changed the share beyond
60 minutes from 10.9 % to 10.6 %. <!-- claim-3, claim-16 --> The 2SFCA uses
counts of hospitals rather than beds or specialists, which the registry does not
record consistently, and a grid four times coarser than the main one. Category
II-1 or above defines complexity by registry category, not by the services
actually available. The OSRM check used a public demo server whose data date is
not published; its responses are archived with the code. Death registration
completeness varies across districts, although its correlation with travel time
was weak; the outcome also depends on the recorded place of death, which is
missing or unclassified for a minority of records. Finally, all results are
ecological and refer to districts, not to individuals [@robinson1950].

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

This study measured, for every Peruvian district, how long residents take to
reach a public complex hospital, weighting a national friction surface by where
the 2025 census places them. About one resident in ten lives more than an hour
away, and the burden falls on the Amazon basin and on the forested slopes
between the Andes and the lowland, where coverage within two hours is lowest.
<!-- claim-1, claim-22 --> Methodologically, the study shows that who counts as
far from hospital care depends less on which hospitals are counted than on how
the population is aggregated and how access is modeled: weighting by where
people live, rather than using district centers, changes the list of deficient
districts by about a third, and a floating catchment measure orders districts
in a way that travel time does not. <!-- claim-13, claim-11 --> These are not
technical footnotes: they decide which places enter a planning list, and anyone
who publishes such a list should state them. Substantively, travel time
was not associated with dying outside a facility among deaths amenable to
hospital care. With a district-level exposure, place of death proved a weak
yardstick for access, and validating access measures in Peru will require
outcomes closer to time-critical care, such as obstetric emergencies or trauma,
and exposures measured on the journeys that patients actually make.

# Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process {.unnumbered}

The authors conceived the study, defined the research questions, the
destinations, the outcome and the analysis plan, took every analytical
decision, approved each analysis gate, and checked the data, code and results
reported here; the interpretation of the findings and the conclusions are
entirely their own. During the preparation of this work the authors used
generative AI tools, under their direct supervision and as technical assistants
only, to assist with writing and debugging code in the analysis pipeline, to
check reference details against the primary sources, and to suggest
alternative wording for parts of the text. These tools took no part in conceiving the study, choosing the methods,
interpreting the results or deciding what to report; every output they produced
was checked against the data or the cited source and edited by the authors, who
rewrote the text as they judged necessary. After using these tools, the authors
reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the
content of the published article.
